archetype.name: Pretender (record ahead of its play)
archetype.definition: A 7-2 team whose efficiency, point differential and yardage profile are those of a league-average club, propped up by a perfect one-score record, a plus turnover margin and a pass rush that makes game-changing plays late.

report.headline: 7-2 on a perfect close-game record; the play says average, the schedule forgives it
report.take:
Denver is 7-2 and tied with Kansas City atop the AFC West, but almost nothing under the hood looks like a 7-2 team. The Broncos have scored 198 and allowed 186, a +12 differential that ranks 15th per game, and their net EPA (0.021) is also 15th. Those are the numbers of a .500 team, and the dossier says so directly: the differential implies 4.7 wins, and Denver's 2.26 wins over expected lead the league. They are a perfect 1.000 in one-score games and covered 77.8% of the time, also first. Bo Nix has started every game, so there is no quarterback split to blame or credit. This is one team, playing coin-flip games and winning every flip.

The winning has a recognizable shape. The defense lives on hitting the quarterback (0.206 QB-hit rate, 2nd; 26 sacks, 3rd) and taking the ball away (13 takeaways, 5th), while the offensive line protects Nix as well as anyone (11 sacks allowed, 2nd). Around those two strengths the team is thin. The offense is 30th in yards per game and 27th in success rate because the run game produces 3.42 yards a carry behind a line that gives backs little room before contact. The defense that ranked 1st in EPA allowed in 2024 and 8th in 2025 has slid to 13th. It is 26th against the run, 31st in missed tackles and 27th in explosive runs allowed. Kansas City ran for 220 in the opener.

Two things complicate a simple regression call. First, this is the second straight year of it: the 2025 team won 14 games on 2.95 wins over expected and an .846 one-score record. A habit of closing, built on a pass rush and a top-11 special-teams unit, may be part skill, though two seasons of it still don't make a third a safe bet. Second, the wins came against real teams. Jacksonville, the Rams, Seattle and Kansas City all have top-six defenses by today's EPA ranks, and the two losses were at Kansas City and at San Francisco, which has the league's top offense. The passing game has also turned the corner lately: three straight positive passing-EPA games, with 30, 28 and 26 points scored.

Where this goes depends less on Denver than on the calendar. Five of the last eight games are against Miami, the Jets, the Chargers and Las Vegas twice, teams with one, two, one and four wins. The close-game luck will probably cool, and the defense is now missing both starting safeties. Even so, a schedule this soft can carry an average team to a playoff-level record. Buffalo at home in Week 16 and the road trips to Pittsburgh and New England are where we find out whether this is a real contender or a well-timed one.

strengths.title: Nix is kept clean
strengths.body: Denver has allowed 11 sacks, 2nd fewest, and the QB-hit rate allowed is 2nd as well, with line penalties also among the fewest. That holds up with a quarterback who holds the ball a while, and it is why Nix can stay ahead of the chains on passing downs when the run game fails. Protection this consistent tends to last, because it rests on the line and the scheme rather than on turnovers or bounces.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: The Broncos hit quarterbacks at the 2nd-highest rate in the league and have 26 sacks, 3rd. The pressure turns into takeaways (13, 5th) and into a deep pass defense that ranks 5th by EPA, because quarterbacks rarely get time to push it downfield. The hits should hold up. The takeaway pace is the less stable part, and losing DE Eyioma Uwazurike to injured reserve thins the rotation.

strengths.title: The passing game is warming
strengths.body: After negative passing EPA against the Chiefs, Chargers and Seahawks early on, Nix has been positive in each of the last three games (2.9, 6.6, 6.6), and the offense scored 30, 28 and 26. Denver passes more than expected (6th in pass rate over expected), which is the right call for an offense that can't run. Whether it lasts depends on Jaylen Waddle, the top target, clearing a concussion.

concerns.title: The record outruns the play
concerns.body: A perfect one-score record and a league-leading 2.26 wins over expected account for the gap between a 7-2 record and a differential that implies 4.7 wins. Some of it may be repeatable closing ability, since 2025 looked the same, but one-score results swing back toward even over time. Expect a loss or two in games they would have won in October.

concerns.title: Soft against the run, sloppy tackling
concerns.body: The defense is 26th in rush EPA allowed, 27th in explosive runs allowed and 31st in missed-tackle rate. Teams that commit to the run move the ball, as Kansas City (220 rushing yards) and the Chargers showed. With both starting safeties out, the last line against those runs gets thinner, so this is a real flaw rather than noise.

concerns.title: An offense that can't stay on schedule
concerns.body: At 3.42 yards a carry, 24th in yards before contact and 27th in success rate, Denver piles up third-and-longs. That shows up in 279.2 yards per game, 30th. The pass protection keeps drives alive, but a run game this weak means few easy points, and margins stay thin even against weaker teams.

trend.note: The offense has improved steadily since a negative-EPA stretch in Weeks 5-6, with positive passing EPA in each of the last three games. The defense is giving up more through the air, though: 272, 321 and 276 passing yards in those same three games.

nextGame.headline: Rested Broncos host a Raiders team that can't stop anyone
nextGame.body:
Denver comes off a bye with 14 days of rest, at home, as a 10-point favorite (moneyline -535, total 40.5). The Raiders score (26.4 points a game, 8th) but can't defend: they allow the most points in the league (29.8), rank 28th in pass EPA allowed, last in short-pass EPA allowed and 31st in success rate allowed. They also can't run, at 3.01 yards a carry with the 32nd run-success rate, which takes away the one plan built to beat Denver's defense. Their weapons are a pass rush that pressures at the 3rd-highest rate and a defense with 14 takeaways, 4th. That is the danger for any offense, even one that protects as well as Denver's.

Availability matters on both sides. Denver will be without both starting safeties, Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones. CB Riley Moss and WR Jaylen Waddle, the top target, are questionable with concussions, and DE Eyioma Uwazurike is on injured reserve. For Las Vegas, Fernando Mendoza started last week after Kirk Cousins started the first nine. TE Brock Bowers is day-to-day with an ankle injury his coach called significant, DE Kwity Paye is questionable with a neck injury, and DT Thomas Booker IV is out.

waysToWin.title: Live underneath against a soft secondary
waysToWin.body: The Raiders allow the worst short-pass EPA in the league and have been torched by opposing WR2s (0.86 EPA per target, 32nd). Even if Waddle sits, Courtland Sutton and Evan Engram can move the chains on short and intermediate throws. That also means Nix gets the ball out before the Las Vegas rush arrives.

waysToWin.title: Hunt a quarterback in transition
waysToWin.body: Las Vegas just changed quarterbacks, and Denver hits the passer at the 2nd-best rate in football. The Raiders' line has kept sacks down, but its QB-hit rate allowed is only 19th. Forcing Mendoza into hurried throws is how Denver's takeaway machine produces short fields.

waysToWin.title: Make them one-dimensional
waysToWin.body: Denver's run defense is its soft spot, but the Raiders are the worst rushing team in the league by success rate and near the bottom by EPA. An early lead forces a quarterback in transition to throw into Denver's pass rush. That is the game script behind a 10-point spread.

waysToLose.title: Giving the ball away
waysToLose.body: The Raiders force turnovers (14 takeaways, 4th) and pressure at the 3rd-highest rate, and turnovers are the one way a bad defense steals a game. Denver's offense doesn't create big margins on its own, so a couple of giveaways can turn a comfortable win into another one-score fight. This time it would be one the Broncos aren't favored to escape.

waysToLose.title: A thin back end gets exposed
waysToLose.body: Without both starting safeties and possibly Moss, Denver's coverage over the middle is vulnerable, and it already allows 0.44 EPA per target to tight ends (28th). If Bowers plays, he is the obvious weapon. Add 31st-ranked tackling and short throws can become long gains.

waysToLose.title: Stalling drives keep it close
waysToLose.body: Denver's run game has rarely worked, and the offense is 27th in success rate. With a low total of 40.5, empty trips let a 4-6 team hang around. The Raiders' 28th-ranked red-zone defense only helps Denver if the Broncos get there often.

nextGame.watch: Who lines up at safety for Denver, and whether Brock Bowers is healthy enough to attack the middle of a secondary missing both starters.

restOfSeason.body:
The close-game magic is the part that won't last. A league-average team doesn't usually keep winning every one-score game, and Denver's turnover margin and league-best ATS rate are the kind of numbers that drift back toward the middle. What should hold is the pass protection, the pass rush's ability to hit quarterbacks, and an offense that has found its passing rhythm lately. The run game and run defense look like structural problems, and the safety injuries make the second one worse until both return.

The schedule is the reason the record should still end up strong. Two games against Las Vegas plus Miami, the Jets and the Chargers are against teams with losing records and mostly bad defenses. Pittsburgh on the road, Buffalo at home and New England on the road are the real tests. Expect a playoff berth on the strength of the slate, and a division race with Kansas City that may come down to tiebreakers. Denver's efficiency profile doesn't suggest a team built to win in January.

confidence.note: Nine games with a consistent profile and one starting QB, but key secondary and receiver injuries are unresolved and close-game luck is hard to time.
